text: Every layer is a memory store [code] [interactive app] The outer-product store reaches its capacity at $M \approx d_k = 64$. The optimal store recalls exactly up to $M = d_k$. Past that, its interference rises from zero like $\sqrt{M/d_k - 1}$, and the store reaches its capacity near $M = 2d_k = 128$, as predicted. Since it cancels a fixed number of memories’ worth of interference, the gap between the two stores shrinks as $M$ grows. This optimal memory store is still linear in the similarities though. It must scale small and large similarities by the same factor. To do better, we need to change how the store recalls. A linear memory store recalls If we had a way to suppress the weight when $k_i\transpose x$ is small, then we can reduce the amount of interference from low similarity keys. Let’s pass each similarity through a nonlinear function $\sigma$ before computing the weighted sum of values: We just rediscovered a two-layer MLP from first principles! The rows of the first weight matrix are the keys, the columns of the second weight matrix are the values. Sukhbaatar et al. pointed out this resemblance between feedforward layers and memory stores, and Geva et al. found that the feedforward layers in trained transformers often work this way, with keys firing on recognizable patterns in the input. Ideally, the gating function $\sigma$ is chosen such that when the similarity is low ($k_i\transpose x \sim 0$ or even when $k_i\transpose x 5 . A squared ReLU activation further suppresses the keys with similarities close to zero. A similarity of 0.1 becomes 0.01, while a similarity of 1 stays 1. In fact, squared ReLUs are one of the lesser known but established-at-scale improvements to MLP activations ( So et al. ). A squared ReLU MLP is a GLU MLP whose gate and input projection share weights, since $\operatorname{ReLU}(Kx)^2 = \operatorname{ReLU}(Kx) \odot Kx$. The SwiGLU MLPs in today’s language models give the gate its own weights and use a Swish activation in place of the ReLU. In practice, MLPs store facts in superposition: many facts share the same weights, and the output is a blend of many memories. Garcia et al. build one explicitly: the hidden units of a GLU MLP compute random features $\phi(x)$ of the input, the second weight matrix is an outer-product store $\sum_i v_i \phi(k_i)\transpose$ over those features, and the MLP stores far more facts than it has hidden units. Still, trained transformers’ ReLU MLPs can activate as few as 1% of their hidden units for a given input, so each recall draws on a small fraction of the memories ( Li et al. ). The original transformer paper made this connection too, but only in v2 and v3 on arXiv. There, Vaswani et al. describe the feedforward layer as “a kind of attention,” with the rows of its two weight matrices as the keys and values, and ReLU in place of softmax. They even tried replacing the feedforward layers with attention over learned key-value parameters, and got about the same translation quality: one version did slightly worse, another slightly better, though the first one trained about 30% slower. The passage is gone from every later version of the paper. We’ll get to how self-attention relates to all this below. Squaring the similarities works because it shrinks low similarity weights much more than large ones. We can push this further with $\sigma(s) = \operatorname{ReLU}(s)^p$. The signal stays the same, since $1^p = 1$, while an interference term with similarity $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ shrinks to $d_k^{-p/2}$. The $M$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference-to-signal ratio is This means the capacity is about memories, geometrically more than before! To check this, we run the same experiment as before for five choices of $\sigma$: Since the interference grows like $\sqrt{M}$, the lines are nearly parallel on a log-log plot. Only their height changes, and with it the capacity, where each line crosses 1: Raising the weights to a power increases the capacity to about $d_k^p$. But what if we could push this to the limit? Rather than pick one power, we can use infinitely many of them. Indeed, the exponential is a weighted sum of every power, with the sharpness $\beta$ setting the weight on the higher powers. Here is the same experiment with $\beta = \sqrt{d_k}$, the value self-attention uses, 6 for the exponential and its series truncated after 2, 3 and 4 terms: With 2 terms, the capacity is about 40, below the linear store’s, since the constant term gives every key a weight of about 1. With 3 terms it’s about 450, and with 4 terms about 3,100, close to the squared ReLU’s. The full exponential stays far below the dashed line, so its capacity is past the edge of the chart. To find the exponential’s capacity, we query with a stored key $k_j$, so the target memory has similarity 1 and weight $w_j = e^{\beta}$. Every other memory has weight $w_i = e^{\beta s_i}$, where for random unit keys the similarity $s_i$ is roughly Gaussian with mean 0 and variance $1/d_k$. With random values of similar lengths, Setting the ratio to 1 gives a capacity of growing exponentially with $\beta$ as long as $\beta$ is well below $d_k$, rather than polynomially in $d_k$ like before! With $\beta = \sqrt{d_k} = 8$, the capacity is about $e^{14} \approx 1.2$ million memories, nearly 20,000 times the linear store’s. A longer run of the same experiment puts the capacity at about 1.2 million too. In practice, we may not want to naively exponentiate numbers in our implementation, since small numbers can underflow and large numbers can overflow. Fortunately, the interference only depends on the ratios between weights, as the chain above shows, so we can divide every weight by their sum without changing the interference-to-signal ratio, while ensuring numerical stability: This is self-attention . 7 Unlike an MLP, whose keys and values are trained weights, self-attention computes its keys and values from the tokens in its context. Each token stores one memory, so the number of memories $M$ is the context length. That’s what makes self-attention non-parametric: its memories aren’t parameters, and the store grows with the context. Here’s the bar figure again, starting with softmax. At $\beta = 8$, recall never fails within the slider’s range, so lower $\beta$ to 2 and raise $M$: recall fails after a few dozen memories. Each doubling of $M$ needs a bit more $\beta$ to keep recall working, which is the idea behind the next section. Since $\beta$ determines how hard we suppress less similar keys, we can increase $\beta$ as the number of key-value pairs increases. Why not just make $\beta$ huge? As $\beta \to \infty$, softmax becomes a hard argmax that picks only the most similar key, which isn’t differentiable, and a very large $\beta$ already makes training work poorly, since the softmax saturates and the gradients to every other key vanish. So we raise $\beta$ only as much as $M$ requires. Scaling the attention logits with $\log M$ is a trick for long contexts that does this. There are a few versions of it, and each sets $\beta$ relative to a fixed reference length $L$, usually the training length, so that $\beta$ keeps its trained value when $M = L$: Here’s how each rule does in our experiment, with $\beta = \sqrt{d_k} = 8$ at $L = 1024$ memories: Qwen’s rule and Su’s rule coincide past the reference length $L$, where the interference-to-signal ratio falls as the store grows, to about 0.004 at 2 million memories. YaRN’s faster-growing scale pushes the ratio down to about $10^{-4}$. In each case, scaling $\beta$ with $\log M$ allows for essentially an unbounded number of memories with distinct keys to be stored. Here are the memory stores we visited, with their capacities when we query with a stored key and the keys and values are random: We started from a heuristic memory store, the outer-product memory, and gradually built our way up to all the standard layers we see today in modern transformers. This perspective also allowed us to estimate how they differ in their capacity, their ability to act as vector-valued key-value stores. I should mention that this capacity estimate is only one way to look at the architecture of modern neural networks. Our capacity estimate only counts how many random vectors a single layer can recall before the interference dominates the signal. In fact we haven’t actually considered the training data at all, which affects what actually is being represented in the keys and values! There are other works which account for the trained layers, measuring stored information in bits. Morris et al. estimate that GPT-style models memorize about 3.6 bits per parameter, and find that once a model fills its capacity, it starts to generalize and memorizes less of each training example. Allen-Zhu & Li find that language models store about 2 bits of factual knowledge per parameter, even when quantized to int8. From here, there are many related directions which are also fascinating: I’ve always been drawn to memory, maybe because I viscerally feel how limited my own is. Perhaps part of me hopes that by understanding how machines remember, I’ll learn something about myself too. Sometimes this accumulation of keys and values is called “Hebbian learning”, since the strength of the synapses (weights) is increased by inputs (keys) and outputs (values) that fire together (are correlated). ↩︎ This outer-product memory store is used for the state of linear attention, also called fast weights: each token stores the memory $(k, v)$ by adding $v k\transpose$ to a matrix that later tokens query ( Katharopoulos et al. ; Schlag, Irie & Schmidhuber ). ↩︎ This is for recalling a clean value vector. If each value only needs to point toward the right answer among a fixed set, like selecting the most likely token, a recall just has to land closer to the right answer than to the wrong ones, and a $d\times d$ matrix can hold about $d^2$ facts ( Nichani, Lee & Bietti ). ↩︎ We can also use this regression objective to design short-term memories that a sequence model writes during the forward pass, like linear attention and self-attention. See my work on test-time regression . ↩︎ For random keys, a ReLU reduces the interference by a factor of $\sqrt 2$. A random key’s similarity is equally likely to be positive or negative, so the ReLU zeroes about half of the weights and leaves the other half unchanged. That halves the interference’s variance, the sum of the squared weights, so the interference itself shrinks by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$. See Zhong et al. for a full derivation. ↩︎ Transformers divide the similarities by $\sqrt{d_k}$ rather than multiplying. But their queries and keys have length about $\sqrt{d_k}$, so a matching pair has $q\transpose k \approx d_k$. Our keys and queries have unit length, so a matching pair has similarity 1. Hence we scale by $\beta = \sqrt{d_k}$ . ↩︎ In transformer notation, the similarity is $k_i\transpose q$ with $q = W_Q x$, scaled by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$. I fold $W_Q$ into the keys. Keys and queries in a transformer have length about $\sqrt{d_k}$, so that scaling matches $\beta = \sqrt{d_k}$ for unit-length keys like ours. ↩︎
